The popular coastal fishing town on the Italian Riviera, which is known for its colourful houses overlooking the sea, has recently introduced no-waiting zones to stop tourists from 'lingering' in popular beauty spots taking pictures. You could now be fined up to 275 euros for {{9}}, which include the most photogenic hotspots. The move has been taken because these areas have become extremely busy, with many people gathering at peak times during the holiday season.

tasks.title: 'A BIG CRAZY ADVENTURE'
body: Over the course of nearly one and a half years, teenage cyclist Liam Garner rode through 14 countries, covering more than 32,000 km in the journey of a lifetime from Alaska to Argentina.

In 2021, Liam had recently graduated from high school and was looking for a “crazy adventure”. He had previously ridden from Los Angeles to San Francisco, and realized that he could pedal across the continent without much difficulty.

After reading a book by an adventurer who had biked from Oregon to Argentina, Liam decided that he would cycle from the point farthest north in the United States to the most southern point in South America.

Liam spent a month preparing for the trip and getting the equipment. He set off on his mountain bike in August, with just a tent, a sleeping bag, a phone, some portable batteries, a first-aid kit, and extra parts for his bike. Other than some food and water, he didn’t have much else. Liam admits that at first his parents were terrified of him taking such a long bike trip, but as he carried on, they became his strongest supporters.

Liam had a riding companion named Logan for eight months of the trip. The two spent over four months biking across Mexico, which was one of Liam’s favourite parts of the trip even though they were robbed in the south of the country. He also admitted that he considered giving up because of the extreme heat every single day.
During the journey Liam was robbed several times, got sick, and had an accident that required surgery. But he kept going through rain, sun, heat, cold, deserts and mountains.

Liam finally arrived in Ushuaia, Argentina on January 10, 2023 – 527 days after he started. He was soon joined by his girlfriend Chloe, and the couple are now backpacking their way back to California.

tasks.title: TOKYO’S BEST ANIMAL CAFÉS
body: Tokyo has a long list of animal cafés. Here are some great spots to visit.

Kotori Café features dozens of colourful parrots, cockatoos and canaries to enjoy afternoon tea with. Don’t expect to see them flying around though, as they’re mostly kept in cages for hygiene reasons.

Meet the resident capybara and its cat friends at Capyneko Café. The South American native animal and the cats will bring plenty of cuteness to your stressful day. Many of the cats here are rescued and adoptable, so let the staff know if you’re interested in giving them a permanent home.

At Mipig Café you can cuddle with adorable miniature piggies. Pet and play with the tiny piglets while sipping a cup of coffee. Note that tickets have to be booked in advance and at least one drink order is required.

Unlike other animal cafés, Dog Heart Café doesn’t have a food or drink menu and you either pay to play with the dogs inside or take one out for a 60-minute walk in the nearby park. You may choose the exact dog you wish to walk.

Hachu Café is a bizarre teahouse, where you’ll be able to enjoy a cup of tea while a reptilian friend observes you from the safety of its transparent box. You can meet a number of reptiles, including lizards, as well as scorpions, turtles and snakes. There’s no cover charge or time limit, – as long as you order a drink.

At ChikuChiku Café cute hedgehogs will welcome you in their tiny dollhouse rooms such as a kitchen, a dining room, or a bedroom. You can feed, touch and take photos of the little cuties in their miniature room-like cages. The entrance fee includes a handful of mealworms to feed to the hedgehogs.

tasks.title: PLAN FOR BIGGEST NESSIE SEARCH IN MORE THAN 50 YEARS
body: It was 90 years ago that Aldie Mackay, {{0}} of the Drumnadrochit hotel, burst into the bar one evening to tell shocked patrons she had just witnessed a “water beast” in Loch Ness.

It was this event that began the modern myth-making around a monster surviving in the depths of the Highland loch – and next weekend {{1}} of Nessie enthusiasts are expected to take part in the biggest organised hunt for the mysterious {{2}} in 50 years.

Organised by the Loch Ness Centre, volunteers from across the globe will participate in person and online in the largest surface watch, searching for breaks in the water and any strange {{3}} over a two-day period.

The hunt will involve {{4}} that has never been used on Loch Ness before, {{5}} drones to produce thermal images of the water from the air, as well as a hydrophone to detect acoustic signals beneath the surface.

Search leader Alan McKenna will inform volunteers live from the Loch Ness Centre each morning about what to look out for and how to record findings. He said: “It’s our hope to {{6}} a new generation of Loch Ness enthusiasts and by {{7}} this large-scale surface watch, you’ll have a real opportunity to personally contribute to this {{8}} mystery that has attracted so many people from around the world.”

tasks.title: APRIL FOOLS' DAY - NO ONE KNOWS HOW IT BEGAN
body: Ever wonder where April Fools' Day came {{0}}? Well, surprise! Nobody seems {{17}} know its true origins. Historians do have some clues, though. In the first place, we do know that April Fools' Day customs date back to {{18}} least Renaissance Europe, but it's likely the tradition originated long before then. Some historians {{19}} recently linked April Fools' Day to the ancient Roman festival of "Hilaria", where at {{20}} end of March, people would come together {{21}} celebrate the god Attis.

Other historians believe April Fools' Day has its origins in the 16th century, when France switched from the Julian calendar to the Gregorian calendar. The Julian calendar began in March and the New Year {{22}} celebrated on March 31. By switching to the Gregorian calendar, the New Year would now {{23}} on January 1.
News traveled slowly back then, and not {{24}} knew when to celebrate the New Year or was willing to change. Those {{25}} continued to celebrate in the spring were often ridiculed and made fun of.
